causalModel.founding: A village grown where nine root-joined trunks stand in one ring; one tree by the Hist's reckoning, nine by the tribes' reckoning.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The ring of trunks encloses firm ground and makes its own stockade, with one gap left unbuilt for a gate. The knoll stands 4.8 m above the water table on firm lowland, with poleable water 32 m west and the Archon-Gideon road 160 m south-west.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A tribe that hosts the convocation's overflow and has grown rich on it, renting pitch-rights to delegations that cannot fit at the Tsoko camp.
causalModel.pressures: Hosting a province's delegations one month a year has made them arrogant the other eleven. Two neighbouring tribes now camp at Greenspring instead, on principle.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A convocation held elsewhere would halve the village. The falling attendance the Root Talk ground counts publicly is already showing in their rents.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: world/sources/catalogue/type-recipes.json hist-village (3-8 villagers; one elevated member on the tree-minder's platform); world/sources/lore/extrapolation/settlement-register.md M3 band 12-35 with guests; UESP Lore:Hist, Lore:Argonian for the tree-minder, the naheesh and the uxith
scaleGrounding.why: Eight resident villagers in five households take the recipe's top band, because the village is rich on rent: the tree-minder and the watcher, the naheesh, the pitch-taker's household and two tribe families. The M3 band is reached only in the convocation month, when up to twelve guests fill the four rented huts and the two pitches. Fourteen structures: nine huts and a round house, the arch, the minder's deck, two shelters and a rack.

candidates.why: A firm-lowland knoll 149 m from the plot: 4.77 m above the water table, ground slope 2.6 deg and 2.17 m of relief across the whole 66 m ring, so eight of the nine trunks sit on a plinth or a pad and the elder trunk needs a dug-in flare. Poleable water 32 m west with the shoreline 40 m off, so the ring encloses firm ground rather than standing in it; the Archon-Gideon road passes 160 m south-west, which is the catalogue's road discovery; flood band 0 and no wet-season inundation.
The flattest ring in the neighbourhood, 1.66 m of relief. Closest to the road at 105 m.
candidates.rejectedBecause: The shoreline is 10 m from the centre, so the western third of a 33 m ring would stand in water. The record's site advantage is that the ring encloses firm ground. This candidate cannot deliver it.

candidates.why: The plotted position: firm lowland, 3.04 m above the water table, flood band 0.
candidates.rejectedBecause: 4.33 m of relief across the 66 m ring, which puts several trunks past the 2 m no-grading limit. The water is 66 m off and the road 241 m off. The macro plot could not see the local relief; the meso pass can.

districts.notes: The ring of nine trunks and the clearing that it encloses: eight huts in eight gaps, the arch in the ninth, the naheesh's house and the minder's deck inside. One kit set; the trunks are landmarks, not buildings.

why.what: The ring: nine Hist trunks on a 21 m radius, eight mud huts in the gaps between them, the arch in the ninth gap and the clearing they enclose.
why.whyHere: The trunks grew here in one ring; the tribe built into the gaps because the ring is a stockade already made.
why.whyNeighbours: The pitch ground lies outside the gate on the road side and the landing on the water side, so both kinds of guest arrive at the one arch.
why.playerPurpose: The safe rest, the services and the lore of the place: every door, the nest, the hearing house and the fighting ground are inside the ring.
why.microGeography: The ring sits on a firm-lowland knoll with 1.5 m of fall from the north-western rise to the southern gap, 4 m above the water table and clear of the wet-season flood.

districts.notes: The rented pitch ground outside the gate on the road side: two shelters, a rack and the pitch line, on the same mud kit set. The canvas is the delegations' own.

why.what: The rented pitch ground: a fenced shelf south-west of the ring with two delegation shelters and a drying rack.
why.whyHere: The village's trade is renting ground to the convocation's overflow. The ground that it rents has to lie outside its own stockade.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies along the spur between the road and the gate, so every payer passes the pitch-taker at the arch while entering.
why.playerPurpose: The ground of Pitch-Rights and Under the Overflow, together with the empty pitches of Water Without Ceremony.
why.microGeography: A shelf at about 3 m, level within half a metre, which sheds south to the road and stays dry when the flats below it flood.

playerPurpose.note: The egg-tenders sell eggs and provisions at the door, the food that can be bought here out of season.

why.whyNeighbours: It shares the elder trunk with the naheesh's house and the eastern guest hut with the rented arc.
why.playerPurpose: The egg-tenders, who sell food at the door out of season and keep the count of which delegations came this year.
why.microGeography: Ground at 3.8 m, a shallow pad; the hut's back wall takes the fall towards the eastern water.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 124.2°, its doorway on 236° onto the ring walk, so a guest steps off the walk into the hut and the rented arc reads as one row.

why.whyNeighbours: It is the first of three rented huts in a row, the row which a walker passes on the ring walk from the gate.

why.whyHere: Two of the four delegations which once paid for huts now camp at Greenspring, so this hut stands empty eleven months and is let in the twelfth.

why.whyHere: A third rented hut is the measure of the village's confidence; the rent ledger shows that it has not been let in two years.
why.whySpot: The south-eastern gap, where the knoll begins to fall to the flats.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the second rented hut and the store hut. The fighting ground of the clearing lies before its door.
why.playerPurpose: The second empty hut of Water Without Ceremony. It is the hut nearest the felling scene.

why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the pitch-taker's hut and the tree-minder's hut on the quiet western arc.
why.playerPurpose: The boat household: the travel service to Uxaneet is asked for at this door.

why.what: The tree-minder's hut, in the gap west of the elder trunk.
why.whyHere: Every Hist village keeps a tree-minder; the office lives against the tree which it keeps.
why.whySpot: The gap west of the elder trunk, so the minder's back wall stands against the elder trunk's root.
why.whyNeighbours: It shares the elder trunk with the naheesh's house. The minder's deck stands across the clearing from its door.
why.playerPurpose: The tree-minder's home in The Child of Two Hist, where the minder's testimony is given.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorframe on one side, so the house is turned until that side opens onto the ring rather than onto the back of the guest huts.

playerPurpose.note: The hearing house of The Child of Two Hist and the evidence socket of the identity case.

why.what: The naheesh's house, the round house at the foot of the elder trunk, where the Root Talk is carried and guests are received.
why.whyHere: The office-holder who carries the Root Talk to the convocation needs a house in which delegations can be heard; the village's standing rests on it.
why.whySpot: It stands inside the ring at the foot of the elder trunk, drawn back off the wall so that the trunk rises clear behind its roof.
why.whyNeighbours: The tree-minder's hut and the eastern family's hut flank it in the wall; the uxith stands to its east and the path from the gate ends at its door.
why.playerPurpose: The hearing house of The Child of Two Hist and the evidence socket of the identity case; the door to which every approach leads.
why.microGeography: It occupies the level 4.0 m floor at the north of the clearing, the highest and driest ground inside the ring.

parcels.orientationWhy: The platform's authored open side faces south-east towards the talk path, while the watcher still looks north across the low deck to the elder trunk.

why.what: The tree-minder's deck, a low woven platform from which the watcher keeps the elder trunk in view.
why.whyHere: The type recipe raises one member of every Hist village onto the tree-minder's platform; here that member is the watcher.
why.whySpot: It stands on the south-western floor of the clearing, off the path from the gate and outside the fighting ground to the east, with the elder trunk 31 m before it.
why.whyNeighbours: The pitch-taker's hut and the chime frame stand behind it and the naheesh's house before it.

playerPurpose.note: The tree-minder is questioned on this deck in The Child of Two Hist.

parcels.orientationWhy: The arch faces on the heartland track's measured 220° bearing, placing its long frame square across the road so a walker passes through the opening rather than round the posts.

why.what: The stick arch which stands across the ninth gap of the ring, the one gap left unbuilt.
why.whyHere: A ring with eight huts in nine gaps needs one gap for a door. A village which lives on guests marks its door.
why.whySpot: The south-western gap faces the spur and the landing path together, so one arch serves both approaches.
why.whyNeighbours: The pitch-taker's hut stands on its right hand and the road-side trunk on its left; the chime frame hangs inside it.
why.playerPurpose: The threshold of the village: the spur passes under it, the ring walk and the path to the naheesh's house begin inside it. The pitch ledger is kept beside it.
why.microGeography: It stands on the 4.1 m lip of the knoll where the spur's climb levels, so an arrival steps through it onto flat ground.

parcels.orientationWhy: The open side of the shelter faces east up the pitch path, so a delegation pitching here looks back down the spur of its arrival.

why.what: The first delegation shelter on the rented pitch ground, an open canvas struck and re-pitched by the month.
why.whyHere: Delegations that cannot fit at the Tsoko camp pitch here and pay for the ground; the canvas is theirs, the ground is the village's.
why.whySpot: The nearer pitch, where the pitch path from the spur ends, on the flat 3 m shelf south-west of the ring.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands inside the pitch line, with the second pitch behind it and the drying rack at the mouth of the ground.
why.playerPurpose: The delegation baggage of Under the Overflow is stacked under this canvas; the container socket sits in it.
why.microGeography: The shelf here is level within 0.5 m over the whole ground and sheds to the south, so the pitch stays dry.

playerPurpose.note: The delegation baggage of Under the Overflow is stacked under this canvas and stays shut.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shelter's authored open side faces north up the pitch ground towards the path, while its canvas ridge runs almost north-south and sheds run-off to either side.

why.what: The second delegation shelter, the further pitch of the ground.
why.whyHere: Two pitches and four huts is the village's capacity; the second pitch is the measure of the overflow for which the village hopes.
why.whySpot: The further pitch stands ten metres beyond its former crowded line on the same shelf, leaving usable ground between the two delegation shelters before the fall to the road.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands behind the first pitch and beside the empty ground on which the two absent tribes once camped.
why.playerPurpose: The empty pitch of Water Without Ceremony and Pitch-Rights: the ground which two tribes left on principle.
why.microGeography: The shelf falls south from the first pitch to the second, so this outer pitch is the first to take run-off in the wet season.

parcels.orientationWhy: The rack turns its open face to the spur, so the rent paid by a delegation hangs in view of the next party up the track; it stands clear of the track's shoulder, on the level strip north of it.

why.what: A drying-rack furnishing at the mouth of the pitch ground, hung with the fish and reed in which a delegation's rent is paid.
why.whyHere: Rent here is paid in kind as often as in coin; the rack is where the kind is seen.
why.whySpot: It stands at the mouth of the pitch ground beside the spur, between the pitch line and the gate.
why.whyNeighbours: The pitch ledger and the pitch-taker stand across the spur from it at the gate.
why.playerPurpose: A read of the village's wealth before the player has spoken to anyone in it.
why.microGeography: It stands on the 3.9 m ground where the spur begins its last climb to the gate.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 105.9° so the doorway looks out at 218° onto the pitch path, the line every delegation walks between the pitches and the village.

playerPurpose.note: The counter sells food, cord and pitch-dues receipts to arriving delegations.

why.what: The pitch store, out of which the village sells food, cord and pitch-dues receipts to the delegations.
why.whyHere: A village that rents standing room to travelling parties sells them what they forgot to bring. The takings are half of what the pitch is worth.
why.whySpot: It stands at the village end of the pitch path, where the rented ground begins.
why.whyNeighbours: The two pitches are downhill of it and the drying rack is beside it, so a delegation passes the counter before it makes camp.
why.playerPurpose: The counter at which supplies are bought. It is also where the pitch-taker can be asked who is camped here.
why.microGeography: A dry hummock above the pitch line, clear of the water that stands in the rented ground.

routes.why: The cart line into the village. The heartland track from the Uxaneet crossing climbs the shoulder from the south-west; the same line is carried inside the boundary, up the last 120 m to the gate gap. It is not a second road beside the track. It is the track, named where the village keeps it.
The trodden ring inside the huts, from which every door in the wall is reached; it begins and ends inside the arch.
The straight walk from the arch across the clearing to the naheesh's door, the spine of the village and the line which every arrival reads first.
The path from the pier head up the bank to the arch: it leaves the water where the bank is low enough to climb with a load.
The short branch from the spur through the gap in the pitch line to the first shelter, worn by baggage carried in and out.

boardwalks.why: A short piled pier from the south bank to the dock at the authored poling channel's natural head, so a boat lands at a deck and not in the reeds.

fences.why: The southern run of the pitch line: the snake fence which marks the rented ground off from the spur, stopping two metres short of the pitch path so a delegation coming up it knows where the paid ground begins. The lower end runs into the wet-season shallows, 4.5 m of it in up to 0.32 m of water. The stakes are driven deep enough to stand through the wet season.
fences.routingWhy: Three short fence modules step down the shelf and turn with its edge, rather than drawing one long panel through more than a metre of fall.

fences.why: The northern run of the pitch line, leaving the ten-metre gap through which the pitch path enters the ground. The whole northern run stands on ground that goes under at the seasonal maximum, 1.28 to 1.52 m of it. The pitch floods every year. The stakes are driven to hold through the flood.

landmarks.notes: The elder trunk: 5.8 m across and 31 m tall at scale 0.55, the beacon of both approaches.

why.what: The elder trunk of the ring, the tallest of the nine Hist columns and the one which the tree-minder watches.
why.whyHere: The village stands here because nine root-joined trunks grew on this knoll in one ring. The elder is the trunk that the tree-minder's deck faces across the clearing.
why.whySpot: The highest trunk stands at the north of the ring on 4.0 m ground, where the knoll is broadest. It is the tallest of the nine at 31 m.
why.whyNeighbours: The naheesh's house stands at its foot inside the ring and the tree-minder's hut in the gap to its west, so the two offices of the village keep the elder trunk between them.
why.playerPurpose: The first thing seen on both approaches, above the canopy from 150 m. It is the mark by which the whole ring is found again after the canopy has hidden it.
why.microGeography: Its base stands on the level 4.0 m floor at the north of the knoll, the broadest firm ground inside the ring; the fall to the south begins beyond the round house.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 2 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 2 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.

why.whySpot: The north-eastern trunk stands on 3.6 m ground, the lowest point of the northern arc, at the head of the fall towards the eastern water.
why.whyNeighbours: It is the corner post of the east family hut and the first guest hut; the woven panels of the wall line run from its bark to both.
why.playerPurpose: A 25 m column of the ring's northern arc. Walking the ring walk, a player counts it second from the elder trunk.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 3.6 m ground, the lowest footing of the northern arc; run-off off the clearing passes its root flare on the way to the eastern water.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 3 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 3 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.

why.whySpot: The eastern trunk stands on 3.9 m ground and is the first of the nine to take the morning light.
why.whyNeighbours: The first and second guest huts are panelled into its bark, so it is the middle post of the rented arc.
why.playerPurpose: A 25 m column on the eastern arc. The ring walk passes its foot between the first and second guest huts.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 3.9 m ground on the eastern slope, where the knoll has given up about half of its 1.5 m of fall.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 4 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 4 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: The ring of nine trunks is the site itself, not a decoration of it. This trunk carries the south-eastern quarter, where the knoll starts to shed towards the flats.
why.whySpot: The south-eastern trunk stands on 3.9 m ground where the knoll begins its fall to the flats.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the second and third guest huts and closes the rented arc at its southern end.
why.playerPurpose: A 25 m column at the south-east. It stands over the point at which the ring walk begins to drop with the knoll.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 3.9 m ground at the point where the knoll turns downward towards the southern flats. The root flare takes the last of the drop.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 5 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 5 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: The trunks came first and the huts were fitted to the gaps between them. This one holds the south of the ring, above the store hut and the road beyond it.
why.whySpot: The southern trunk stands on 3.5 m ground, the lowest footing of the nine. It is the trunk seen from the road.
why.whyNeighbours: The third guest hut is panelled to its northern side and the store hut to its southern, so it divides the rented gaps from the tribe's own stores.
why.playerPurpose: A 25 m column at the south. From the Archon–Gideon road it is the trunk nearest to a traveller. It stands over the store hut's blank wall.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 3.5 m ground, the lowest footing of the nine. Wet-season run-off leaves the clearing past it.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 6 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 6 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: Nine trunks grew root-joined on the knoll. Two of them stand either side of the gate. This is the road-side post of that gap.
why.whySpot: The trunk on the road side of the gate stands on 3.9 m ground and is the left-hand post of the entrance for a walker.
why.whyNeighbours: The store hut is panelled to one side of it. On the other side the wall line stops, because the next gap is the gate.
why.playerPurpose: The left-hand post of the gate for a walker coming up the spur. It is the mark by which the arch is found from the pitch shelf.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 3.9 m ground on the rise out of the southern low point, so the arch beside it stands a little above the road side of the ring.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 7 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 7 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: The trunks are the reason for the settlement. This is the water-side post of the gate gap. It is the first of the nine that a boat party passes.
why.whySpot: The trunk on the water side of the gate stands on 4.4 m ground and is the right-hand post of the entrance for a walker.
why.whyNeighbours: The gate gap lies to its north and the pitch-taker's hut to its south, so it is the post that a walker passes on the right hand under the arch.
why.playerPurpose: The right-hand post of the gate. The landing path bends round it before the arch opens on the left hand.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 4.4 m ground, at the point where the landing path finishes its climb from the pool.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 8 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 8 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: The nine trunks stand on a 21 m radius. This one has the highest footing of them, on the western rise which keeps the pool clear of the ring.
why.whySpot: The western trunk stands on 5.0 m ground, the highest footing of the nine, on the rise which the western pool skirts.
why.whyNeighbours: The pitch-taker's hut and the west family hut are panelled into it. Their two doors open onto the clearing either side of it.
why.playerPurpose: The column with the highest footing of the nine, at 5.0 m. A player passes it on the outer walk between the pool and the ring.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 5.0 m ground on the western rise. The pool lies 60 m west-north-west and about 3.8 m below it.

landmarks.notes: Ring trunk 9 of nine: 4.7 m across and 25 m tall at scale 0.45, 14.4 m from each neighbour along the chord.

why.what: Trunk 9 of the nine Hist columns which stand in one ring on a 21 m radius.
why.whyHere: The trunks decided the plan of the village. This one stands on the north-western rise which shelters the ring from the west.
why.whySpot: The north-western trunk stands on 5.0 m ground beside the tree-minder's hut, on the rise which shelters the ring from the west.
why.whyNeighbours: The west family hut stands to its south and the tree-minder's hut to its north, so it is the post between the boat household and the minder.
why.playerPurpose: A 25 m column at the north-west. The tree-minder's hut is panelled to it, so a player following the ring walk finds the minder's door at its foot.
why.microGeography: Its base is on 5.0 m ground on the north-western rise, where the ring's 1.5 m of fall begins; it ends at the southern trunk.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the elder and north-eastern trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the elder and north-eastern trunks.
why.whyHere: The dispute rests on the joins: one tree by the Hist's reckoning, nine by the tribes'. This one lies behind the hut of the egg-tenders, who are asked about it most often.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the elder and north-eastern gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: Eight joins lie behind the eight built gaps. This one sits behind the east family hut, the first gap clockwise from the elder trunk.
why.playerPurpose: A waypoint on the outer walk round the ring. It is the join nearest to the elder trunk for a player who is asked to count the trees.
why.microGeography: The swell lies along the ring's tangent on the level 4.0 m northern floor, where there is little fall for it to shed.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the north-eastern and eastern trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the north-eastern and eastern trunks.
why.whyHere: Root joins are the evidence in the village's long argument over whether nine trees stand here or one. A delegation lodged in the first guest hut is shown this one on arrival.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the north-eastern and eastern gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the first guest hut, one of eight joins spaced round the ring. The gate gap, two-thirds of the way round, has no join at all.
why.playerPurpose: A player walking outside the wall sees this join and the back of the first guest hut in one view.
why.microGeography: It lies along the tangent on 3.6 m ground and turns the clearing's run-off round the eastern side of the first guest hut.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the eastern and south-eastern trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the eastern and south-eastern trunks.
why.whyHere: The joins carry the argument between the Hist's count of one tree and the tribes' count of nine. This is the join at which the felling claim is made.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the eastern and south-eastern gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It sits behind the second guest hut. The gate gap has no join, which is the gap the tribes cite when they count nine trees.
why.playerPurpose: The join at which the felling claim is argued in One Tree or Nine; the evidence socket sits on it.
why.microGeography: It lies on the eastern slope at about 3.8 m, its uphill face part buried and 2.8 m of swell standing on the downhill side.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the south-eastern and southern trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the south-eastern and southern trunks.
why.whyHere: The tribes count nine trees and the Hist's reckoning is one; the joins are the ground on which the two counts meet. This is the fourth join clockwise from the elder trunk.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the south-eastern and southern gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the third guest hut at the end of the rented arc. It pairs with the join behind the store hut, on the far side of the southern trunk.
why.playerPurpose: One of the eight joins counted on the outer walk. It sits where the ground begins to fall, so the swell shows more of its bulk on the downhill side.
why.microGeography: On the south-eastern fall it lies across the shoulder of the drop, so wet-season water passes on both sides of the third guest hut.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the southern and road-side trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the southern and road-side trunks.
why.whyHere: A join is the place at which two of the nine share a root, which is the reason the Hist's reckoning gives one tree. This one lies behind the store hut.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the southern and road-side gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the store hut on the road side of the ring, the last join a walker meets before the gate gap, which has none.
why.playerPurpose: The join a player passes between the road spur and the gate; a walker who leaves the track early meets it before the arch.
why.microGeography: The southern ground is the lowest of the ring at 3.5 m. The swell stands clear of the store hut's plinth, which is not undercut in the wet season.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the water-side and western trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the water-side and western trunks.
why.whyHere: The joins are the physical claim: root running unbroken from one trunk to the next. This one lies on the pitch-taker's side of the ring, where delegations pass it on the outer walk.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the water-side and western gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the pitch-taker's hut, the first join past the gate gap for a walker going clockwise round the outside.
why.playerPurpose: A landmark of the outer walk on the pitch side of the ring. It is the join nearest to the pitch path.
why.microGeography: It lies along the tangent on about 4.2 m ground on the western climb, above the level of the pitch shelf.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the western and north-western trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the western and north-western trunks.
why.whyHere: A visitor who disputes the count is taken outside the wall to see a join. This one lies behind the boat household's hut.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the western and north-western gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the west family hut, between the joins of the pitch-taker's gap and the tree-minder's gap.
why.playerPurpose: A landmark of the outer walk on the western arc. It is the join by which a player returning from the pool rejoins the ring.
why.microGeography: On the western rise at about 4.8 m, with the swell's flank turning run-off away from the west family hut's plinth.

landmarks.notes: Root swell outside the wall line between the north-western and elder trunks; 6.5 x 4.6 x 2.8 m at scale 0.45.

why.what: A root swell which lies along the ring outside the wall, joining the bases of the north-western and elder trunks.
why.whyHere: Both counts of the trees, the Hist's one and the tribes' nine, are argued from the joins. The tree-minder names them for guests. This join lies behind the minder's own hut.
why.whySpot: It lies on a 27.5 m radius outside the hut in the north-western and elder gap, clear of the wall so that a walker outside the ring sees the join and the hut behind it together.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies behind the tree-minder's hut and closes the round of eight at the foot of the elder trunk.
why.playerPurpose: The last of the eight joins on the outer walk, at the foot of the elder trunk.
why.microGeography: It lies on the north-western fall from 5.0 m towards the elder trunk's floor, along the slope rather than across it.

landmarks.notes: The nest totem, north-east in the clearing between the naheesh's house and the family hut.

why.what: The totem of the uxith, the village nest, turned to face the gate across the clearing.
why.whyHere: A Hist village keeps its nest inside the enclosure of its tree; the enclosure is defended for the nest's sake.
why.whySpot: It stands on the north-eastern side of the clearing, between the naheesh's house and the first family hut, off the paths and out of the fighting ground to the east.
why.whyNeighbours: The two households charged with the eggs, the naheesh's and the eastern family's, have their doors within twelve paces of it.
why.playerPurpose: The mark by which the player reads that the ring is a nest and not a market. It is also the gated social reward of the type recipe: entry is social, not mechanical.
why.microGeography: It stands on the level northern floor of the clearing at 4.0 m, the driest ground inside the ring.

landmarks.notes: Chimes stacked eleven months of the year and hung inside the gate for the convocation month; in the convocation variant.

why.what: The frame from which the bone chimes hang inside the gate, dressed for the convocation and bare the rest of the year.
why.whyHere: Chimes at the threshold are the Hist-village custom of the region; a village that hosts delegations dresses its threshold more than most.
why.whySpot: It stands inside the gate to the right of the path to the naheesh's house, so that an arrival passes it without walking into it.
why.whyNeighbours: It sits between the gate and the pitch-taker's hut, whose household hangs and strikes the chimes.
why.playerPurpose: The first sound of the village on arrival in the convocation month. In the other eleven months it is a silent frame, which tells the player which month it is.
why.microGeography: It stands on the 4.2 m floor just inside the gate, where the ground levels after the climb from the spur.

docks.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/tamu_wooddock01

why.what: The landing at the natural head of the authored poling channel south of the nine-trunk ring, where the boat from Uxaneet ties up.
why.whyHere: The village is reached by water from Uxaneet as often as by the road. The dock follows the independently solved channel endpoint (fit `to-water`), rather than moving that waterway to validate a preselected berth.
why.whyNeighbours: The pier runs from it to the bank and the landing path climbs from the bank to the arch; the western family's hut, whose household poles the boat, stands in the wall above it.
why.playerPurpose: The arrival point for a player who comes by boat and the travel service to Uxaneet.
why.microGeography: Piles stand at the channel head south of the ring; a short pier makes the last crossing to its bank and the land path climbs north-west to the arch.

combatSpaces.why: The eastern floor of the clearing, between the naheesh's house and the rented arc: where the felling claim of One Tree or Nine is argued and where a rite which goes wrong is fought, with the hearing of The Child of Two Hist held on the same ground.
The arch and the ground either side of it: the single gap in the stockade, where a wary village turned hostile holds its line and through which a night raid comes.
The open pitch ground between the shelters and the spur, where the baggage of Under the Overflow is opened and a rent dispute in Pitch-Rights comes to blows.

approaches.sequence: From the fork off the Archon-Gideon road the top of the elder trunk shows above the mangrove canopy, 31 m against 10 m at 116 m off; the track drops into low ground and the canopy closes over it for 60 m; at the pitch ground the whole ring rises as one grey wall of trunks and hut roofs; then the arch reads as the single gap in it, with the chime frame inside; through the arch the path runs straight to the round house.
approaches.wayfinding: Keep the tallest trunk ahead; the arch is the single gap in the wall. The path through it runs to the round house.
approaches.notes: The catalogue's road discovery. The spur bends twice, at the pitch ground and at the foot of the knoll, so the gate is not seen from the road; the elder trunk is.

approaches.fromDirection: south, up the authored poling channel from the Uxaneet water network
approaches.sequence: From the water south of the ring the nine trunks stand above the reeds like the teeth of a comb, the elder trunk tallest among them; as the boat noses to the pier the bank's mangroves take them one by one; from the pier head the southern gap and wall read together above the bank; the landing path climbs north-west to the arch.
approaches.wayfinding: From the pier, climb towards the gap in the trunks; the arch is round the trunk on the right.
approaches.notes: The travel service from Uxaneet lands here. The bank stands 2 m above the water at the pier head and the path rises under a metre in 50 m; the arch is hidden from the pier by the bank's mangroves and re-found at the bend.

interiorClaim.owner: the naheesh who carries the Root Talk

travelServices.timetable: on request; hourly during the convocation

occupants.cultureRole: naheesh who carries the Root Talk

assetConstraints: district.nine-trunks.ring is one kit set (settlement-mud-v1). Every piece inside the ring comes from it: huts, round house, arch, deck, totem, chime frame, woven panels. No root-kit walkway or house form stands inside the ring.

the nine trunk columns and eight root joins are landmarks from the tropical set (anvilgianttrunk, anvil_root01, one author, composited together in flora-province-v1) at a uniform scale of 0.45 (0.55 for the elder trunk); no piece is attached to them, so no piece is asked to span between two trunks

the delegation canvas on the pitch ground is the mud kit's open shelter (argoniantent02), which has no interior and so no door; the closed tent (argoniantent01) is not used because it would need an interior claim a canvas cannot honour
the naheesh's round house (bmv hutexterior) is a shell in its kit; its interior is claimed from dungeon-root-v1 pending an owner decision on the medium Argonian hall interior

provision.notes: LH51 takes the pitch ground, the ledger station at the gate and the pitch-taker's hut; LH52 takes the eastern root join and the felling scene on the eastern floor of the clearing; LH53 takes the baggage under the first shelter and the pitch-taker's household; LH37 takes the two empty rented huts and the empty pitch; MQ19 takes the naheesh's house, the tree-minder's hut and the minder's deck.

networkTerminals.why: The heartland track reaches the village on the shoulder that carries a cart above the pool's flood line; it crosses the boundary here and the spur carries it the last 120 m to the gate gap, so track and street are one line.
The dock and pier meet the independently solved poling channel at its south-side natural head; the land path carries baggage north-west to the ring gate.
